{
  "title": "Introduction to Transaction Processing Concepts and Theory",
  "description": "An 8-week intermediate course for university students covering the fundamental concepts of database transaction processing, including concurrency control, recovery, ACID properties, schedules, serializability, and transaction support in SQL.",
  "sections": [
    {
      "title": "Module 1: Fundamental Concepts of Transaction Processing",
      "topics": [
        "Single-User vs. Multiuser Systems",
        "Understanding Concurrency: Interleaved and Parallel Processing",
        "Defining a Transaction and its Boundaries",
        "A Simple Model of a Database for Transactions",
        "Core Database Operations: read_item(X) and write_item(X)",
        "The Need for Concurrency Control",
        "Concurrency Problem 1: The Lost Update Problem",
        "Concurrency Problem 2: The Temporary Update (Dirty Read) Problem",
        "Concurrency Problem 3: The Incorrect Summary Problem",
        "Concurrency Problem 4: The Unrepeatable Read Problem",
        "The Need for System Recovery",
        "Common Causes of Transaction Failure"
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Module 2: Transaction States and System Recovery Concepts",
      "topics": [
        "The Transaction as an Atomic Unit of Work",
        "Transaction States: Active, Partially Committed, Committed, Failed, Terminated",
        "State Transition Diagram for Transaction Execution",
        "Key Operations for Recovery: begin, commit, rollback (abort)",
        "The System Log (Journal) and its Role in Recovery",
        "Types of Log Records",
        "Using the Log for Recovery: Undo and Redo Operations",
        "Defining the Commit Point of a Transaction"
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Module 3: Desirable Properties of Transactions (ACID)",
      "topics": [
        "Introduction to the ACID Properties",
        "A - Atomicity: All or Nothing",
        "C - Consistency Preservation: From One Valid State to Another",
        "I - Isolation: Concurrent Execution without Interference",
        "D - Durability: Ensuring Changes are Permanent"
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Module 4: Characterizing Schedules based on Recoverability",
      "topics": [
        "Defining a Transaction Schedule (History)",
        "Understanding Conflicting Operations in a Schedule",
        "Recoverable Schedules: Ensuring Commits are Valid",
        "Cascading Rollbacks and Cascadeless Schedules",
        "Strict Schedules: Preventing Dirty Reads and Writes",
        "Comparative Analysis of Schedule Types"
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Module 5: Characterizing Schedules based on Serializability",
      "topics": [
        "Serial vs. Nonserial Schedules",
        "Defining Serializable Schedules",
        "Schedule Equivalence: Result Equivalent vs. Conflict Equivalent",
        "Conflict Serializable Schedules",
        "The Importance of Serializability for Database Consistency",
        "Testing for Conflict Serializability: The Precedence Graph",
        "Algorithm for Constructing and Interpreting a Precedence Graph",
        "Case Study: Analyzing Schedules for Serializability using Precedence Graphs"
      ]
    },
    {
      "title": "Module 6: Transaction Support in SQL",
      "topics": [
        "Transaction Management in SQL: COMMIT and ROLLBACK",
        "Implicit Transaction Initiation",
        "The SET TRANSACTION Statement",
        "SQL Isolation Levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED",
        "SQL Isolation Levels: REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE",
        "Potential Problems at Lower Isolation Levels: Dirty Read",
        "Potential Problems at Lower Isolation Levels: Nonrepeatable Read",
        "Potential Problems at Lower Isolation Levels: Phantoms",
        "Example of a Complete SQL Transaction"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
